2023_24_8_b_24680_troy_school_district_a.paragraph: Plante & Moran, PLLC's Report to the Board of Education accompanies the audit of Troy School District's basic financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2023, covering Results of the Audit, Other Recommendations and Observations, and Informational Items. The letter, dated October 3, 2023, reports no disagreements with management and states that management corrected all accumulated misstatements. The most consequential figure is a General Fund fund balance of approximately $32,620,000 at June 30, 2023, equal to 17.2 percent of expenditures or approximately 8.9 weeks of operation, against a statewide average of approximately 20.30 percent at June 30, 2022.
2023_24_8_b_24680_troy_school_district_a.page:
**What it is**
Report to the Board of Education from Plante & Moran, PLLC on the audit of Troy School District's basic financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2023. Cover letter and audit report both dated October 3, 2023, signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager. The firm thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the business office.

| Section | Pages |
| --- | --- |
| Results of the Audit | 1-4 |
| Other Recommendations and Observations | 5-6 |
| Informational Items | 7-16 |

**Results of the Audit**
Engagement letter dated May 31, 2023; planning meeting August 4, 2023. The audit was also conducted under Government Auditing Standards, with a separate letter dated October 3, 2023 on internal control over financial reporting and compliance. Significant accounting policies appear in Note 2; no new policies were adopted during 2023. The most sensitive estimates were the District's shares of MPSERS net liabilities under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75: $340,447,659 for pension and $19,240,985 for OPEB at June 30, 2023, from Office of Retirement Services data. No disagreements with management, no significant difficulties, no consultations with other accountants; management corrected all identified misstatements.

**Other Recommendations and Observations**
- GASB Implementation Guide Update 2021-1: grouped purchases individually below the capitalization threshold but above it in aggregate must be recorded in fixed asset records; effective for the year ending June 30, 2024.
- The Food Service Fund balance continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum of three months' operating expenditures; the spenddown plan with the Michigan Department of Education should continue.
- Troy Career Center (MiWorks) federal and state expenditures are entered manually into an Excel template serving as the subsidiary ledger, including the WIOA program tested in the single audit; automation or more frequent reconciliation is encouraged.
- The Inflation Reduction Act, signed August 16, 2022, allocated $369 billion over the next 10 years toward reducing emissions approximately 40 percent by 2030, and offers tax-exempt entities a direct-payment option for qualifying capital improvements.

**Informational Items - state funding**
For 2022/2023 all schools except hold harmless districts were funded at a target foundation allowance of $9,150 per pupil, an increase of $450 per pupil. For 2023/2024 the target rose $458 per pupil to $9,608, a 5 percent increase; cyber schools remain at $9,150. The blended count stays 90 percent October 2023 and 10 percent February 2023, with a new two-year 50/50 blend under Section 29 for declining enrollment districts. State special education support moves fully to Section 51 rather than Section 20, so foundation dollars no longer supplement the Headlee Amendment obligation. Also noted: Section 31a At-Risk on an opportunity index, Section 31d universal free breakfast and lunch, GSRP eligibility raised to 300 percent of poverty, a riders-per-square-mile transportation formula, and a 5 percent ISD operations increase. Federal pandemic education aid ends September 30, 2024; the next Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference is January 2024.

**MPSERS and fund balance**
At September 30, 2022 the MPSERS net pension liability was approximately $37.9 billion, up approximately 57 percent from $24.2 billion at September 30, 2021; the net OPEB liability was approximately $2.1 billion, up approximately 40 percent from $1.5 billion. The plan returned 27.2 percent for the year ended September 30, 2021 versus a 4.8 percent investment loss for the year ended September 30, 2022. During 2022/2023 General Fund expenditures exceeded revenue by approximately $361,000, reducing fund balance to approximately $32,620,000 at June 30, 2023 - 17.2 percent of expenditures, approximately 8.9 weeks of operation.

**Also covered**
GASB financial reporting model project (final standards targeted March 2024); Revenue and Expense Recognition possibly issued during 2027; sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023; GASB Statement No. 101 effective for the year ending June 30, 2025; Treasury Numbered Letter 2023-1; arbitrage; cybersecurity; and real estate strategy through Plante Moran Cresa.
2023_24_8_b_24680_troy_school_district_a.verbose:
Report to the Board of Education, Troy School District, June 30, 2023, issued by Plante & Moran, PLLC in connection with the audit of the School District's basic financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2023. The transmittal letter, dated October 3, 2023, states that in addition to the audit report the firm is providing the results of the audit, a summary of unrecorded possible adjustments, other recommendations and observations, and informational items, paginated as Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-16). The firm thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness. The Results of the Audit letter is signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager.

RESULTS OF THE AUDIT. Plante & Moran audited the financial statements of Troy School District as of and for the year ended June 30, 2023 and issued its report thereon dated October 3, 2023. As stated in the engagement letter dated May 31, 2023, the auditor's responsibility is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management with Board oversight are fairly presented in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, obtaining reasonable but not absolute assurance. Internal control was considered solely to determine audit procedures. The audit was also conducted in accordance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, under which the firm issued a separate letter dated October 3, 2023 regarding internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements. The audit followed the planned scope and timing communicated at the planning meeting on August 4, 2023.

Significant audit findings. Significant accounting policies are described in Note 2; no new accounting policies were adopted and the application of existing policies was not changed during 2023. No transactions lacked authoritative guidance or consensus, and none were recognized in a different period than when they occurred. The most sensitive estimates were the School District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for the pension and other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75: $340,447,659 for the pension plan and $19,240,985 for the OPEB plan as of June 30, 2023, based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services. Disclosures were characterized as neutral, consistent, and clear. The auditors encountered no significant difficulties, reported no disagreements with management, and stated that management corrected all accumulated known and likely misstatements other than trivial ones. Representations were requested in the management representation letter dated October 3, 2023, and there were no consultations with other independent accountants. The firm read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and nothing came to its attention suggesting the other information was materially misstated or inconsistent with the financial statements.

OTHER RECOMMENDATIONS AND OBSERVATIONS. GASB Implementation Guide Update 2021-1 clarifies that items purchased in a group that are individually below a district's capitalization threshold but exceed it in the aggregate should be reported in fixed asset records; the guidance takes effect in the year ending June 30, 2024, and the District should review its practices and written policies. Food Service Fund - Fund Balance: the fund balance continues to exceed the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures, and the District should continue to monitor the spenddown plan entered into with the Michigan Department of Education. Troy Career Center (MiWorks) Expenditure Reporting: the allocation is tracked manually, with the program director entering all federal and state expenditures into an Excel template that serves as a subsidiary ledger by program, including the WIOA program tested as part of the single audit; the firm encourages a more automated process or more frequent reconciliation. Inflation Reduction Act: signed into law August 16, 2022, the IRA allocated $369 billion over the next 10 years for energy and climate projects intended to reduce emissions by approximately 40 percent by 2030, and includes a direct-payment option in lieu of a nonrefundable tax credit for tax-exempt entities; qualifying capital expenditures may include certain electric vehicles and renewable energy equipment such as solar panels.

INFORMATIONAL ITEMS. Managing the Changing Financial Resources Landscape describes the period since 2020 - pandemic uncertainty, a significant infusion of federal resources, and a stable and growing state budget platform. The May 2023 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference predicted sufficient resources for current programs with substantial resources for new initiatives, and the 2023/2024 School Aid Bill was completed and signed into law. For 2022/2023, following the May 2022 conference, all schools except a few hold harmless districts were funded at the target foundation allowance of $9,150 per pupil, and all schools including hold harmless districts received an increase of $450 per pupil, the largest per-pupil increase since the start of Proposal A (1994/1995), with added funding for special education, At-Risk, wraparound services such as nurses and counselors, and the Great Start Readiness Program consistent with the School Finance Research Collaborative. For 2023/2024 the target foundation allowance increases by $458 per pupil to $9,608, a 5 percent increase, with hold harmless districts also receiving $458 while cyber schools remain at $9,150. The blended pupil count continues at 90 percent weighting for the October 2023 count and 10 percent for the February 2023 count, with a two-year blend for declining enrollment districts qualifying under Section 29 based on 50 percent of the blended 2022 count and 50 percent of the blended 2023 count. State special education funding moves entirely to Section 51 of the State Aid Act rather than partly from Section 20, so special education is fully categorical and no longer supplements Headlee Amendment payments from foundation allowance amounts. Other provisions: GSRP reimbursed at the target foundation allowance with income limits raised to 300 percent of the poverty level; Section 31a/At-Risk weighted by an opportunity index; Section 31d universal free breakfast and lunch; a riders-per-square-mile transportation formula; one-time funding for student mental health, school safety, and a student loan repayment program; increased retirement system contributions despite discontinuation of the one-time $1 billion contribution made in 2022/2023; and a 5 percent increase in the intermediate school district operations allocation. The May 2023 conference projected 2024, 2025, and 2026, with a substantial 2023 surplus carrying into 2024, a reduced 2024 surplus because of one-time payments, and a return to significant surplus in 2025; inflation and a potential recession are the two key risks, and the next conference occurs in January 2024. Education-focused federal pandemic funding concludes September 30, 2024, the "federal funding cliff," raising questions about the ESSER III/11t allocation, staff retention and recruitment, pupil count trends, learning loss, expanded GSRP preschool, food service redesign, inflation-driven cost increases, technology, and school security and mental health costs.

Michigan School Meals. Beginning in 2023/2024, free breakfast and lunch are available to all Michigan students, state funded for those who do not qualify under the National School Lunch and National School Breakfast programs. Participation is not automatic; districts must apply using the 2024 Coordinated Application in the State's NexSys system, participate in the National School Lunch Program, serve breakfast and lunch at no cost to pre-K through 12th grade students, adopt the Community Eligibility Provision (CEP), collect family income information, and write off all outstanding student negative balances, which the Food Service Fund is not allowed to absorb.

MPSERS net liabilities. The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2022 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $37.9 billion, an increase of approximately 57 percent from $24.2 billion at September 30, 2021, driven largely by net investment losses; the plan's annual investment rate of return was 27.2 percent for the year ended September 30, 2021 compared with an investment loss of 4.8 percent for the year ended September 30, 2022. The retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB liability of approximately $2.1 billion at September 30, 2022, an increase of approximately 40 percent from $1.5 billion at September 30, 2021, for the same investment reasons.

Fund Balance. During the 2022/2023 school year the School District's General Fund expenditures exceeded revenue by approximately $361,000, reducing the General Fund fund balance to approximately $32,620,000 at June 30, 2023. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2022 was approximately 20.30 percent of expenditures and outgoing transfers, which would approximately equal average operating costs for a 10-week period. The School District's fund balance percentage is 17.2 percent and equals approximately 8.9 weeks of operation.

Other informational items. The GASB financial reporting model project began August 2013; the exposure draft "Financial Reporting Model Improvements" was issued June 2020 with a comment period ending February 2021, and the GASB's goal is final standards by March 2024; at its June 2023 meeting the board tentatively decided to remove governmental fund reporting issues from the scope. A related project, the June 2020 preliminary views titled "Revenue and Expense Recognition," could produce a standard during 2027. Sinking fund legislation effective August 6, 2023 allows millages approved by voters after May 7, 2023 to fund student transportation vehicles and related parts, supplies and equipment, and trucks and vans registered under the Michigan vehicle code, 1949 PA 300, MCL 257.1 to 257.923; sinking funds authorized prior to March 29, 2017, between March 29, 2017 and May 7, 2023, and after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for separately, each with its own balance sheet and statement of revenue, expenditures, and changes in fund balance, and an annual independent sinking fund audit is required. GASB Statement No. 101 on compensated absences is effective for the year ending June 30, 2025. Michigan Department of Treasury Numbered Letter 2023-1, to be released during fiscal year 2023/2024, supersedes Bulletin 7 and Numbered Letter 2004-4 and takes effect for sinking fund and bond compliance audits reported for the June 30, 2024 reporting period; the completion date will always be the June 30 immediately following the later of the certificate of substantial completion or 95 percent of bond proceeds being spent, districts will submit an annual transmittal letter instead of bond closeout financial information, and levies renewed after May 7, 2023 must be accounted for in a separate capital projects fund. Arbitrage is addressed, including the computation generally completed at the five-year anniversary of the original bond sale and amounts due back to the Internal Revenue Service. On data security, the report cites the K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021 signed into law in October 2021, warns that passwords like "August2023" are easily guessed, and raises questions about phishing awareness and PII and FERPA data storage. On real estate strategy for owned assets, the firm offers an introduction to its affiliated entity, Plante Moran Cresa.

2023_25_aug_2023_financial_statement.verbose:
Monthly financial reporting package for Troy School District covering the period July 1, 2023 through August 31, 2023, presented as a Statement of Revenues and Expenditures for each fund and marked unaudited. Every statement pairs an Approved Budget column, dated 6/13/23, against year-to-date actual amounts through August 31, 2023.

GENERAL FUND. Budgeted revenue by source is Local Sources 43,788,278; State Sources 123,125,300; Federal Sources 7,980,072; and Interdistrict Sources 12,137,782, for Total Revenues of $187,031,432. Actual receipts for the two-month period are Local Sources 7,406,575; State Sources shown as a dash, meaning nothing recorded; Federal Sources 125,465; and Interdistrict Sources 61,472, for Total Revenues of $7,593,512. On the expenditure side, Instruction is budgeted at Basic Programs 90,145,544, Added Needs 30,445,199, and Adult Education 945,357, for Total Instruction of 121,536,100; actual instruction spending is Basic Programs 899,647, Added Needs 571,808, and Adult Education 122,834, for Total Instruction of 1,594,289. Support Services are budgeted and actual as follows: Pupil 14,522,814 budget and 69,277 actual; Instructional Staff 11,599,560 and 1,111,084; General Administration 1,719,578 and 266,480; School Administration 9,708,700 and 831,037; Business Services 1,499,207 and 310,768; Operations 14,159,333 and 2,620,007; Pupil Transportation 4,330,166 and 164,679; Central Services 3,781,018 and 824,334; and Support Services (Athletics and Other) 2,444,783 and 250,388, for Total Support Services of 63,765,159 budget and 6,448,054 actual. Revenues Over (Under) Expenditures is $1,049,692 in the budget column and $(457,216) actual, so General Fund spending exceeded receipts over the first two months of the fiscal year, largely because state aid payments had not yet begun while payroll and operations spending had.

CONSOLIDATED DEBT SERVICE FUNDS. Revenues are budgeted at Local Sources 30,440,000 and State Sources 275,000, with actual Local Sources of 5,109,665 and no State Sources recorded. SPECIAL REVENUE FUND - TROY PRESCHOOL FUND (531). Revenues budget and actual: Local Sources 2,439,589 and 302,644; State Sources 1,356,025 with nothing recorded. Expenditures budget and actual: Salaries 1,181,956 and 76,487; Employee Benefits 647,927 and 47,273; Purchased Services 826,452 and 31,531; Supplies and Materials 138,000 and 35,134; Capital Outlay 25,000 and 3,701; Other 1,000 and 2,625; Debt Service 490,065 with nothing recorded. Total Revenue $4,845,000 and $824,644; Total Expenditures $4,930,000 and $1,993,151; Revenues Over (Under) Expenditures $(85,000) budget and $(1,168,507) actual. Sinking fund construction spending is running well ahead of levy receipts at this point in the year, producing the largest actual deficit of any fund in the package.

Overall, the package shows a district two months into the fiscal year with substantial local revenue recorded in the debt service, capital projects, and sinking funds, no state aid payments yet recorded in the General Fund, Food Service Fund, or Troy Preschool Fund, and no debt service principal or interest payments yet made. The Troy Career Center Fund is exactly in balance, the Community Service and Troy Preschool funds are running surpluses, and the General Fund, Food Service Fund, 2019 Capital Projects Fund, and Sinking Fund are all reporting expenditures in excess of revenues.

2023_26_11072023_policy_update_recommend.paragraph: A memorandum dated November 7, 2023 from Rick West of the Troy School District Business Office (4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098) to the Policy Committee transmits Policy Manual updates recommended by Miller Johnson School Policy Services and the Cabinet team, organized by manual section with an explanation for each change. Proposals span the 2000 through 8000 series and add stand-alone policies on electronic signatures, school visitors, and engagement with outside organizations. The most consequential provision requires each school building to maintain at least two functioning epinephrine auto-injectors and at least one functioning opioid antagonist, administered by trained personnel, with 911 called for a suspected opioid overdose.
2023_26_11072023_policy_update_recommend.page:
**Origin**
Memorandum from Rick West, Business Office, 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098 (phone 248.823.4022, fax 248.823.4013), to the Policy Committee, dated November 7, 2023, re: Policy Manual Recommended Updates. Changes were recommended by Miller Johnson School Policy Services and the Cabinet team. Each item carries an Action block with lines for Cabinet, Policy Committee, and Board of Education; the Cabinet position is filled in on every item while the Policy Committee and Board of Education lines are blank.

**2000 series - students, health and safety**
- Update 15.01 (Policy 2000.01 Admission and Enrollment): adds a Home Schooled Students provision to the Resident Students section, under which the Board will attempt to accommodate home-schooled students wishing to take non-essential elective classes, citing MCL 380.1561 and MCL 388.1766b.
- Update 15.03 (Policy 2000.07 / Administrative Regulation 2007-AR Health and Safety): combines opioid antagonist language with the existing Epi-Pen policy. Each building must maintain at least two functioning epinephrine auto-injectors and at least one functioning opioid antagonist; trained personnel or authorized contractors administer them; parents are notified; the District will call 911 for a believed opioid overdose and encourage treatment through a program licensed under part 62 of the Public Health Code, 1978 PA 368. The stated purpose is compliance with sections 1178 and 1179 of the Revised School Code, with regulations incorporating the Michigan Department of Education's Medication Administration Guidelines. Cabinet: Supports (Adopt language in its entirety).
- Update 15.04 (Policy 2000.07 Health and Safety): clarifies that annual notice and parental opt-out for physical examinations and screenings do not apply to sports physicals.

**3000 and 4000 series**
- Update 15.06 (Policy 3000.03 Instruction): commits the District to provide homebound and hospitalized instruction to qualified students consistent with federal and state law.
- Update 15.07 (Policy 4000.02 Employment Considerations): adds "pregnancy status" to the prohibited bases for employment discrimination and harassment, cross-referencing Policy [8000.07].
- Update 15.09 (Policy 4000.04 Evaluations, Discipline and Discharge, Resignations): requires a rigorous, transparent, and fair evaluation system with annual year-end evaluations, and provides that the Superintendent's evaluation follow state law and/or the employment contract, that Board members receive training in the evaluation framework, and that untrained members be recused.
- Update 15.10 (Policy 4000.05 Other Matters of Employment): states mandatory reporting duties reflecting the Child Protection Law.

**5000 series - business**
- Update 15.11 (Policy 5000.03 Purchasing): requires administrative regulations and effective internal control over state and federal grants and awards. Cabinet: Supports (Adopt language in its entirety).
- Update 15.12 (Policy 5000.07 Risk Management): requires a District-provided form for injury to students, staff, or visitors.
- Update 15.13 (Policy 5000.12 Use of Electronic Signatures, NEW): authorizes acceptance, distribution, and reliance on electronic records and electronic signatures unless prohibited by law.

**6000, 7000 and 8000 series**
- Update 15.14 (Policy 6000.02 / Administrative Regulation 6002-AR Safety and Security): revised for threat situations, adding a Threat Assessment section requiring a Superintendent-developed protocol. Cabinet: Supports (Also maintain current Firearms and Weapons language).
- Update 15.16 (Policy 7000.12 School Visitors, NEW, cited as Policy 7012): authorizes the Superintendent or building principal to bar or expel disruptive persons and request law enforcement assistance.
- Update 15.17 (Policy 7000.13, NEW, cited as Policy 7013, "Engagement with Outside Organizations"): requires review of requests from civic institutions, charitable organizations, and outside groups.
- Update 15.18 (Policy 8000.03 / Administrative Regulation 8003-AR): Section 504 and ADA Title II nondiscrimination, naming the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services as Compliance Officer for employment issues and the Director of Special Education for FAPE and accessibility, and permitting service animals as required or permitted by law.
- Update 15.19 (Policy 8000.07 / Administrative Regulation 8007-AR): responds to the Elliott Larsen Civil Rights Act amendment signed by Governor Whitmer, effective 2024, adding sexual orientation and gender identity/expression.
- Update 15.20 (Policy 8000.09 Digital Communications): adds a Public Use section declaring District social media a limited public forum and listing prohibited content categories.
2023_26_11072023_policy_update_recommend.verbose:
Memorandum on Policy Manual Recommended Updates from Rick West, on Troy School District Business Office letterhead showing 4400 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098, phone 248.823.4022, fax 248.823.4013, addressed to the Policy Committee and dated November 7, 2023. It outlines proposed updates to the District's Policy Manual as recommended by Miller Johnson School Policy Services and the Cabinet team, with explanations for each contemplated change, broken down by section of the manual; two leading sections carry the note that there are no recommended updates. Each recommendation ends with an Action block listing Cabinet, Policy Committee, and Board of Education, with the Cabinet position recorded for every item and the other two lines left blank.

Update 15.01 (Policy 2000.01 Admission and Enrollment). Because clients raised questions about home-schooled students, language is added to the Resident Students section: the Board will attempt to accommodate students who are home schooled and have a desire to take non-essential elective classes in the School District in a manner consistent with the law, with administrative regulations as needed. Citations given are MCL 380.1561 and MCL 388.1766b. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.03 (Policy 2000.07 / Administrative Regulation 2007-AR Health and Safety). Responding to renewed client interest in opioid antagonists, the recommendation combines opioid antagonist language with the existing Epi-Pen policy and regulation in Policy 2007 and 2007-AR. The School District will acquire or purchase and maintain at least two functioning epinephrine auto-injectors (epi-pens) and at least one functioning opioid antagonist for and at each school building it operates. Properly trained School District personnel or authorized contractors will administer an opioid antagonist to any individual on school grounds believed to be having an opioid-related overdose, an epi-pen injection to any individual believed to be having an anaphylactic reaction, or to any student with a prescription on file. The District will notify the parent of any student to whom it administers an epi-pen injection or opioid antagonist on school grounds or at a school-related activity. For a believed opioid-related overdose, the District will encourage parents or legal guardians to seek treatment from a substance use disorder services program licensed under part 62 of the Public Health Code, 1978 PA 368, and will call 911. The stated purpose is compliance with sections 1178 and 1179 of the Revised School Code; the policy creates no rights or remedies, and the Superintendent will promulgate administrative regulations incorporating by reference the Michigan Department of Education's Medication Administration Guidelines. Cabinet: Supports (Adopt language in its entirety).

Update 15.04 (Policy 2000.07 Health and Safety). To resolve confusion about the Physical Examinations and Screenings policy, a proviso is added: annual notice will be given to parents of any health or physical examinations or screenings, parents may opt their students out of all such examinations and screenings, and the policy is not intended to apply to physical examinations required for sports participation. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.06 (Policy 3000.03 Instruction). A specific policy on homebound instruction: the School District will provide homebound and hospitalized instruction to qualified students consistent with federal and state law and other applicable guidance, with administrative regulations as needed. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.07 (Policy 4000.02 Employment Considerations). Two recent federal legislative changes clarified the prohibition on discriminating against employees or prospective employees on the basis of pregnancy, so the Discrimination and Harassment policy in the Personnel section is supplemented. The revised language bars discrimination or harassment in employment on the basis of race, color, national origin, religion, sex, marital status, pregnancy status, genetic information, disability, age, or any other illegal grounds, and cross-references Policy [8000.07]. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.09 (Policy 4000.04). Added to the Evaluations, Discipline and Discharge, Resignations policy. The District will use a rigorous, transparent, and fair evaluation system complying with Michigan law and including annual year-end evaluations for all teachers and administrators unless otherwise permitted by law. The system is intended to improve performance and encourage professional growth, and also to result in separation from employment of those who, after notice and an opportunity to improve, continue to be ineffective. Evaluation of the Superintendent is to be conducted consistent with state law and/or the employment contract; Board members must receive training in the evaluation framework for the Superintendent before participating in an annual performance evaluation, and any Board member who does not obtain the training in advance shall be recused. Cabinet: Supports (Adopt language in its entirety).

Update 15.10 (Policy 4000.05 Other Matters of Employment). A mandatory reporting statement capturing the spirit of the Child Protection Law: each professional staff member and all other employees who are mandatory reporters and/or who have reasonable cause to suspect child abuse or neglect shall report immediately every case, ascertained or suspected, of abuse or neglect resulting in physical or mental injury to a student by other than accidental means. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.11 (Policy 5000.03 Purchasing). The Superintendent will promulgate legally compliant administrative regulations concerning expenditures of funds received through state and federal grants and awards, and shall establish and maintain effective internal control over grants and awards providing reasonable assurance that programs and funds are managed in compliance with applicable statutes, regulations, and award terms and conditions. Cabinet: Supports (Adopt language in its entirety).

Update 15.12 (Policy 5000.07 Risk Management). The Board seeks to minimize risk in all operations through planning that accounts for the safety of students, employees, and the public, protection of District property, and avoidance of financial loss or liability. The Superintendent is responsible for a risk management program including means for identifying, eliminating, reducing, or transferring risk, and may provide for purchase of insurance. In the event of injury to students, staff, or any visitor to school grounds, a School District provided form shall be completed by the appropriate staff member. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.13 (Policy 5000.12 Use of Electronic Signatures, NEW). A stand-alone policy inserted at the end of the 5000 series. Unless a provision of law specifically prohibits use of an electronic record for the specified purpose, the Board authorizes acceptance and distribution or transmission of electronic records and electronic signatures to and from District staff and other persons and between staff members, and authorizes staff to create, send, receive, store, process, use, and rely upon them. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.14 (Policy 6000.02 / Administrative Regulation 6002-AR). Policy 6000.02, Safety and Security, and its administrative regulation are significantly revised to address threat situations. Facilities and grounds will be kept safe, secure, clean, and attractive, and the Superintendent will implement a maintenance program providing for regular inspection and periodic maintenance of all facilities, compliant with applicable safety, health, and environmental requirements. The District will undertake reasonable cooperative efforts with law enforcement agencies, and the Superintendent and building administrators determine when law enforcement presence is necessary. Under Threat Assessment, the Superintendent will develop a threat assessment protocol for situations posing a threat to the health, safety, and welfare of the school community, aimed at preventive or corrective measures, protecting potential victims, and assisting the student being assessed. Cabinet: Supports (Also maintain current Firearms and Weapons language).

Update 15.16 (Policy 7000.12 School Visitors, NEW). A stand-alone policy in the 7000 series, cited in the text as Policy 7012 and entitled "School Visitors." Visitor guidelines keep the educational program undisturbed and prevent intrusion of disruptive persons. The Superintendent or building principal may prohibit entry of any person or expel any person when there is reason to believe the person's presence would be detrimental to the good order of the school, and if the individual refuses to leave or creates a disturbance the principal may request whatever assistance is required from the local law enforcement agency. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.17 (Policy 7000.13, NEW). A stand-alone policy in the 7000 series, cited as Policy 7013 and entitled "Engagement with Outside Organizations." Any request from civic institutions, charitable organizations, or outside groups involving contests, exhibits, sales of products to and by students, promotional materials sent home with students, graduation prizes, fund raising, and free teaching materials must be carefully reviewed to ensure such activities promote student interests without advancing the special interests of any particular group. Cabinet: Supports.

Update 15.18 (Policy 8000.03 / Administrative Regulation 8003-AR). Addressing recurring service animal questions covered by the Americans with Disabilities Act and existing Policy 8000.03. In accordance with Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 and Title II of the ADA, no otherwise qualified individual with a disability shall, solely by reason of disability, be excluded from participation in, denied the benefits of, or subjected to discrimination; the District does not discriminate in admission, access, participation, or treatment of students with disabilities, nor against any job applicant or employee with a disability. The District has developed guidelines for providing a free appropriate public education (FAPE) under Section 504 and the ADA. The Superintendent appoints the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services as Compliance Officer for employment issues and the Director of Special Education as Compliance Officer for FAPE and other accessibility issues, and will develop a complaint procedure. Service animals will be permitted to the extent required or permitted by law, with administrative regulations governing non-service animal requests. Cabinet: Supports (Adopt language in its entirety).

Update 15.19 (Policy 8000.07 / Administrative Regulation 8007-AR). The Michigan Legislature passed and Governor Whitmer signed an amendment to the Elliott Larsen Civil Rights Act expanding protections for LGBTQ individuals; although it does not take effect until 2024, modification of Policy 8007, Discrimination and Harassment, is recommended now, with "pregnancy status" already addressed in the Series 4000 updates. The revised policy bars discrimination and harassment on the basis of race, color, national origin, religion, sex (including sexual orientation and gender identity/expression), marital status, pregnancy status, genetic information, disability, age, or any other basis prohibited by law, and designates the Assistant Superintendent of Employee Services to supervise implementation. Cabinet: Supports (Adopt language in its entirety).

Update 15.20 (Policy 8000.09). In response to issues associated with public interaction on district social media, Policy 8000.09, Digital Communications, is revised to include a new "Public Use" section. Digital communication occurring on District premises or using District equipment is governed by the Acceptable Use Policy and this policy, which also applies off District premises and on non-District equipment; communication between staff and students, and between staff and parents, community members, and other adults, should be professional and of the same content, tone, and demeanor as in-school communication. District social media, to the extent open to the public, collectively constitutes a limited public forum, and all comments and postings are subject to monitoring and, where permitted, removal. Public posts must address District business, and the District may remove content that is off-topic, abusive, illegal, obscene or sexually explicit, campaigning for or against political campaigns, candidates, or ballot measures, compromising to safety or security, containing personal identifying or sensitive personal information such as doxing, commercial such as solicitation or advertisement, or copyrighted, trademarked, or otherwise legally protected. Users who repeatedly or egregiously violate the guidelines may be banned from posting or commenting, and the Public Use portion must be displayed to users or made available by hyperlink.
